06-061.r: VIBGYOR is the order of increasing wavelength (violet shortest, red longest) and decreasing frequency; so red's wavelength is more than violet's.

06-065.r: Light's energy ∝ 1/wavelength: among blue, green, yellow and red, blue has the highest energy and red the lowest.

06-066.r: A glass prism deviates violet most and red least: red travels fastest in glass, so glass has its lowest refractive index for red.

06-067.r: A false: red (≈ 700 nm, 1.77 eV) has less energy than green (≈ 530 nm, 2.34 eV). R true: red's wavelength is longer.

06-068.r: The Sun is seen a few minutes before actual sunrise (and after sunset) because of refraction of light in the atmosphere.

06-069.r: The Sun and Moon look elliptical near the horizon because of refraction.

06-070.r: Stars twinkle due to atmospheric refraction: starlight passes through layers of changing refractive index, so its apparent position keeps shifting.

06-071.r: Red is used in traffic signals because it has the longest wavelength, is scattered least and is seen clearly from far away.

06-072.r: Danger signals are red because red light (longest wavelength) is scattered least by air molecules and is seen from far: A and R true, R explains A.

06-074.r: The sky looks blue because blue (short-wavelength) light is scattered most by air molecules (Rayleigh scattering).
06-074.h: Short waves scatter most (blue sky); long red waves scatter least (red danger signals).

06-078.r: True: blue sky and red Sun at sunrise/sunset are due to scattering (statements 1 and 3). False: rainbow colours are not caused by scattering.

06-080.r: Sky looks dark at very high altitudes because the air is very rare and scattering is not prominent: both true, (ii) explains (i).

06-081.r: An astronaut sees the sky black: space has no atmosphere, so there is no scattering of sunlight (from a very high plane it also looks black).

06-083.r: The sea looks blue due to reflection of the sky and scattering of light by water; blue light (short wavelength) scatters most easily.

06-084.r: Grass looks green because it reflects green light and absorbs all other colours; a black surface reflects none, a white one reflects all.

06-085.r: Colours of a soap film on water in daylight → interference of light reflected from its outer and inner surfaces.

06-086.r: Rocket moving away from Earth at 2/10 the speed of light: its blue light (450–490 nm) shifts to longer wavelength → looks yellow-orange from Earth.

06-087.r: Convex mirror, object anywhere between infinity and pole → image between pole and focus behind the mirror: virtual, erect and diminished.

06-088.r: Black strips painted on a convex lens only block part of the light: the image is still a full horse, just less bright.

06-089.r: Rear-view mirror in vehicles → convex mirror: always an erect, diminished image with a wider field of view.
06-089.h: Convex = see more: wider field of view for traffic behind.

06-092.r: Concave mirror gives a real, inverted, same-size image when the object is at the centre of curvature.

06-093.r: Image larger than oneself → concave mirror (surface curved inwards); used in torches, searchlights, headlights and as shaving mirrors.

06-094.r: Shaving mirror → concave (large focal length): a face between focus and pole gives an enlarged, erect, virtual image.

06-095.r: Searchlights and car headlights → concave mirror: a bulb near the focus gives a parallel beam that lights far ahead.

06-097.r: Dentist's mirror → concave mirror: an object closer than the focal length gives a magnified, upright image of the tooth.

06-100.r: Umbrella against sunlight: white on top (reflects most radiation), black underneath (absorbs whatever passes through).

06-101.r: Astronomical telescope (two convex lenses: objective and eyepiece) forms a final image that is inverted, virtual and highly magnified.

06-102.r: A larger objective lens diameter gathers more light → the telescope's resolution (resolving power) increases.

06-103.r: A plane mirror is a spherical mirror with infinite radius of curvature → its focal length is infinite and its power zero.

06-104.r: An object between two parallel plane mirrors forms infinite images (each image is the image of another image).

06-106.r: Rotating a plane mirror by angle θ turns the reflected ray by 2θ.

06-107.r: Glass beads on traffic signals glow by total internal reflection (light in denser glass beyond the critical angle): A and R true, R explains A.

06-108.r: The seven colours of white light are separated by a prism: each colour (wavelength) is refracted by a different amount.

06-109.r: Rainbow order VIBGYOR: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange, red → 'blue, green, yellow' is in correct order.

06-110.r: Rainbow → dispersion, refraction and internal reflection of sunlight in raindrops (all three); it appears opposite the Sun.

06-111.r: Dispersion (splitting white light into its component colours) is done by a prism.

06-112.r: Middle colour of the rainbow (fourth of the seven in VIBGYOR) → green.

06-113.r: The end colour bands of a rainbow → violet and red.

06-114.r: A rainbow forms opposite the Sun, so at 12 noon (Sun overhead) it cannot be seen.

06-115.r: Shadows form due to rectilinear (straight-line) propagation of light blocked by an opaque object.

06-116.r: A swimming pool looks shallower than it is due to refraction: light from the bottom bends away from the normal going from water to air.

06-117.r: A slanting stick in water looks short and bent due to refraction, not scattering: A true, R false.

06-118.r: Both true (refraction): a coin in water looks closer than it is; a coin above water, seen from under water, looks higher than it is.

06-119.r: An air bubble in water acts as a concave (diverging) lens, because air's refractive index is lower than water's.
06-119.t: The bubble's surface is convex, yet it behaves as a concave lens.

06-121.r: Convex and concave lenses of the same focal length in contact → combined focal length infinite → act as a plane glass sheet.

06-122.r: Minimum height of a plane mirror to see one's full image = half the person's height (angle of incidence = angle of reflection).

06-123.r: Full-length image needs a mirror half the person's height: 1.50 m ÷ 2 = 0.75 m.

06-124.r: Radius of curvature of a plane mirror is infinite (it is a spherical mirror of infinite radius; image as far behind as the object in front).

06-125.r: Magnifying glass → convex lens (makes objects look larger).

06-126.r: Long-sightedness (hypermetropia: far objects clear, near ones blurred) is corrected with a convex lens.

06-127.r: Not true for hypermetropia: 'a concave lens corrects it' (a convex lens does). Far objects clear; near-object image forms behind the retina; eyeball is shorter.

06-128.r: Reading glasses → convex (converging) lens, thicker in the middle; it also corrects far-sightedness.

06-129.r: Myopia is reduced with a concave lens.

06-130.r: Myopia (near-sightedness: near objects clear, distant ones blurred) is corrected by a concave lens.

06-133.r: Myopia → concave lens; hypermetropia → convex lens.
06-133.h: MyoCAVE: Myopia → conCAVE; the other one (hypermetropia) gets convex.

06-134.r: Dark adaptation: bright light bleaches rhodopsin in the rods; sight in the dark returns as rhodopsin re-forms (minutes), helped by the pupil widening.
06-134.c: The book accepts (a), (c) and (d). The slow part of dark adaptation, taking minutes, is the rebuilding of bleached rhodopsin in the rods, option (c); the pupil widens within seconds.

06-135.r: The eye focuses by changing the convexity (shape) of its lens; the bending power of cornea and humour stays constant.

06-136.r: Ciliary muscles change the eye lens's curvature and so its focal length; relaxed → thin lens, longer focal length for distant objects.

06-137.r: Not correct: ENT doctors use a concave head mirror (small central hole), not convex. Mirage – total internal reflection; searchlight – concave; summer – light-coloured clothes.

06-138.r: Least distance of distinct vision (near point) for a normal eye ≈ 25 cm, denoted D.

06-141.r: Power of a lens is measured in dioptre: P = 1/f (f in metres); converging lens positive, diverging lens negative.

06-143.r: Focal length f (cm) = 100 ÷ power (dioptre) → a +2 dioptre lens has focal length 100/2 = 50 cm.

06-145.r: Young's double slit: fringe width β = λD/d = 500 nm × 1 m ÷ 1 mm = 0.5 mm.

06-146.r: Exposure ∝ (1/f-number)² × time: f-8 at 1/250 s gives the most (≈ 0.000062), more than f-22 1/60, f-16 1/125, f-5.6 1/1000.

06-147.r: The retina works like the film of a traditional camera; its nerve cells turn light into electrical impulses sent via the optic nerve.

06-148.r: The human eye forms the image of an object on the retina; the optic nerve carries it to the brain (the eye works like a camera).

06-150.r: Long-sightedness (hypermetropia): image of a near object forms behind the retina (eyeball too short); corrected by a convex lens.

06-151.r: An opaque object's colour = the colour of light it reflects (the rest is absorbed).

06-152.r: Colour TV makes all colours from three basic colours: red, green and blue (phosphor 'triads' in the CRT).

06-154.r: Red, green and blue lights on the same spot (equal proportions) give white light: they are the additive primary colours.

06-155.r: Black is not a primary colour. Primary colours of light: red, green, blue; in painting: red, yellow, blue.
06-155.t: Don't confuse light primaries (red, green, blue) with painting primaries (red, yellow, blue).

06-157.r: Pigment primaries cyan, magenta, yellow: magenta + yellow → red; cyan + magenta → blue (both statements true).

06-158.r: Magenta → red + blue; teal → blue, green, white; mauve → blue, red, white; cyan → green + blue.

06-159.r: Sunlight (white light) has seven colours, VIBGYOR; splitting it with a prism is called dispersion.

06-160.r: Odd one out: brown, which is not among the seven VIBGYOR colours of white light.

06-161.r: Optical illusions: size of the Sun at dusk, colour of the Sun at dawn, twinkling of stars (1, 2, 4); not the Moon at dawn or the Pole Star.
